transcript: Meeting header: Dec 2, 2025 • 16:30 UTC • Duration 47m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Laura (HorizonEd Head of Platform), Tom (SRE), Priya (PM)
Summary (auto-generated): walkthrough of Console debugging: request playback, request inspector, error analysis, rollbacks and canary routing; agreed next steps for POC and security docs

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. We'll take you through the Redwood Console debugging flows — request playback, request inspector, and how we triage errors end-to-end. Ethan will drive the demo.

[00:18] Laura Chen: Great — high level we want to see how quickly our SREs can go from an alert to a reproduce-able request and then to a remediation path. Latency and cost tradeoffs matter but reliability is priority.
[00:35] Ethan Cole: Yep, totally. Quick note on context: you're on Hosted today, you mentioned some noisy 500 spikes last week on the /summarize endpoint — Tom, is that right?

[00:45] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, we had this burst around 2am local. Some users saw timeouts. Our monitoring flagged increased tail latency and error ratio. We couldn't repro locally and logs were kinda sparse — that's why the request-level playback and traces matter.

[01:05] Maya Patel: Also to call out we'll show automatic trace correlation — console pulls request logs, KV cache hits, and model variant metadata into a single pane so you can see route, model, prompt, and token breakdown in one place.

[01:22] Ethan Cole: Jumping in — opening Console -> Requests -> Request Inspector. You'll see a list of request IDs, filters for status, model, region, and a timeline. I'll filter to errors in the last 24 hours and the /summarize route.
[01:40] [audio glitch] Speaker 2: sorry there's a tiny audio pop. Ethan, can you slow a touch?

[01:45] Ethan Cole: Sure. So here's an example request ID: r-20251202-4a7c. The inspector shows the request payload (prompt truncated), the model variant (gpt-open-3q, quantized), and the request lifecycle: queued -> started -> backend-error.
[02:10] Priya Nair: That lifecycle is great. Can we see the full token-level breakdown and where time was spent?

[02:18] Ethan Cole: Yup — there's a timeline view: tokenization, pipeline, kernel exec, and network time. In this case the kernel exec was short but we see higher than normal network wait due to retries to a fallback region.
[02:36] Laura Chen: Wait — retries? We thought we had a single-region constraint on hosted. How are retries happening?

[02:44] Maya Patel: Good Q. Redwood will retry across compatible variants if the primary model fails and if your routing policy allows fallback. For your enterprise plan we can lock routing to region-only or disable automatic fallback for compliance.
[03:00] Tom Alvarez: Hmm we need no cross-region retries for regulated customer data. Is that a per-route toggle?

[03:07] Ethan Cole: Yes, in Console -> Routes you can pin region and disable fallback. We'll also show how audit logs record that decision so your security team can prove no outbound cross-region requests occurred.

[03:25] [00:03:25] Ethan Cole: Now playback — hit the Playback button and Console will re-run the request in a sandboxed execution, with identical headers and optional env flags. Playback shows stderr and structured model outputs plus a side-by-side diff of responses.
[03:45] Priya Nair: Is playback deterministic? We can't re-run with user PII in prompts in prod. How do you handle sensitive data?

[03:55] Maya Patel: Great point. Playback supports two modes: redacted replay and synthetic prompt replay. Redacted removes PII via rules (emails, SSNs) and replaces tokens; synthetic swaps user content with fixtures. You control retention and replays.

[04:18] Ethan Cole: Watch the error trace here: backend-error originates from a token overflow in a downstream microservice call we do via function-calls. The console links to the function call logs and shows that the microservice returned a 502 which we mapped to a 500 in the Redwood layer.
[04:40] Tom Alvarez: That mapping concerns me. Can we configure mappings so our stack alerts on the original microservice status?
[04:48] Ethan Cole: Yes — you can set custom status mappers in the route policy. We'll add that to the POC checklist.

[05:00] [00:05:00] Ethan Cole: Switching to Traces tab — you'll see spans per subsystem: Router, Runtime, Kernel, Network, Cache. We correlate KV cache hits; this request shows a low cache-hit rate which increased compute and exposed a microservice instability.
[05:22] Laura Chen: So this could be load-related — we had a config that raised TTLs recently. Can Console surface a delta comparison across time windows?
[05:31] Ethan Cole: Yes, the Optimize tab suggests cache configs and shows historical hit-rate deltas. It can propose increasing prefix caching for /summarize to reduce token compute.
[05:45] Priya Nair: Are those suggestions safe to apply automatically? We need guardrails.
[05:51] Maya Patel: They are suggestions only; you can auto-apply within strict policy bounds (e.g., only for non-PII routes) or run as a canary on 5% traffic first.

[06:08] [00:06:08] Ethan Cole: Now I'll demo Error Analysis workspace — it aggregates all 5xx and 4xx spikes, groups by root cause fingerprinting (stack traces, model variant, route). It surfaces the top 3 offending request patterns and lets you drill into sample requests.
[06:30] Tom Alvarez: The grouping looks useful. How noisy is the fingerprinting? We don't want false-positive groups.
[06:36] Ethan Cole: Fingerprinting is configurable; you can tune sensitivity. We also let you upload custom regex rules to group by your own error fields.

[06:50] [00:06:50] Laura Chen: Walk us through a real triage: we find a spike, we identify representative request, we reproduce via playback, then we update route or model. How fast can that go in a mature flow?

[07:03] Ethan Cole: In our experience teams can go from alert to reproduction in under 15 minutes if they have request IDs in alerts and appropriate permissions. Playback reduces finger-pointing because you get an executable reproduction locally or in a sandbox.
[07:18] Priya Nair: Permissions — RBAC — do we get token-level audit trails?
[07:23] Maya Patel: Yes, audit logs include who played back a request, what flags were used, and any auto-applied config changes. KMS keys used for model logging are logged too.

[07:35] [00:07:35] Ethan Cole: Quick pause — I'm going to intentionally reproduce the 502 by toggling a simulator for the downstream function we call. Playback will show the function's stderr and the point of failure.
[07:52] [sound of typing]

[08:00] Ethan Cole: There — playback reproduces the 502. You can see in the console the span with the microservice call and the payload. Click 'Open logs' and it opens the raw log lines with fuzzy transcription artifacts sometimes present depending on ingestion.
[08:20] Tom Alvarez: I see the log lines but some hostnames look like they're truncated — the ingestion pipeline sometimes elides long hostnames. Is there a raw export?
[08:28] Ethan Cole: Yes — Export -> Raw logs (GZIP) gives you full lines. We recommend piping that into your SIEM for long-term retention.
[08:40] Laura Chen: For the POC, can we export a sliding window of last 48h logs and a sample of low-latency and high-latency requests?
[08:48] Maya Patel: Absolutely — Ethan will include the export template in the follow-up.

[09:00] [00:09:00] Ethan Cole: Next, playback diff view — if the reproduced response differs we show token-level diffs and a confidence delta. This helps identify model regressions when you rollout a new variant.
[09:15] Priya Nair: How do you capture model rollouts? We have canary policies in our infra and want to tie into that.

[09:23] Ethan Cole: Redwood has rollout policies integrated with routing. You can create canaries (5/10/20%) per model version; Console shows per-segment metrics and automatically votes to roll back if latency or error thresholds breach.
[09:40] Laura Chen: That auto-vote — is it auditable? We need to be able to roll back manually too.
[09:46] Maya Patel: It's auditable and reversible. You can set it to manual rollback or auto with guardrails. All actions are in the audit trail.
[10:00] [00:10:00] Tom Alvarez: Two security questions: 1) Where are logs stored and how long? 2) Can playback run against an on-prem private connector so data never leaves our VPC?

[10:10] Ethan Cole: Logs live in your chosen retention bucket — hosted customers get a default 30d but you can extend. For Private deployment we can keep logs entirely in your VPC; playback can be executed via a private connector so no plaintext leaves your network.
[10:28] Maya Patel: We'll include a network diagram in the docs. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and KMS customer-managed keys for logs at rest.

[10:40] [00:10:40] Ethan Cole: Another neat tool: Request Timeline playback — a flame chart per request that shows where latency accumulates across subsystems. In this sample, we see small spikes on the kernel exec but majority of time was queueing due to a cold-start on a model variant.
[10:58] Laura Chen: Cold-starts — can Optimize recommend warm pools for certain models?
[11:05] Ethan Cole: Yes — Optimize suggests warm pool sizes and estimated cost delta. It also simulates expected tail latency improvements.
[11:20] Priya Nair: Cost estimates — are those token-level only or include infra?
[11:26] Maya Patel: Cost reports show token cost, GPU time estimates, and per-request infra overhead so you can see full economics of a warm pool vs increased latency.

[11:40] [00:11:40] Ethan Cole: Quick demo on Alerts: you can configure an alert that includes a direct link to the representative request and automatically attaches the playback snapshot and relevant trace spans to your ticketing system.
[11:55] Tom Alvarez: That would save time — our tickets usually lack request IDs.
[12:01] Ethan Cole: We also have a webhook enrichment feature: when an alert fires we'll call your ticketing endpoint with attached artifacts and a small redacted payload for debugging.
[12:15] Laura Chen: Any quirks with function-calls data? We have heavy use of external function calls and want to keep those traces clean.
[12:22] Ethan Cole: We capture function-call metadata and surface the call stack. For privacy you can opt to only keep metadata (status, duration) and drop payloads.
[12:35] [00:12:35] Priya Nair: Walkthrough for SRE onboarding — how long to train new engineers on Console?
[12:42] Maya Patel: Most teams ramp in 1-2 weeks with guided runbooks. We provide runbooks for common playbooks like triage, canary rollback, and cache tuning.

[12:55] Ethan Cole: I'm going to show a cached vs non-cached replay. Toggle 'enable prefix cache' in the playback options and re-run the request; you'll see token compute and cost delta in the results.
[13:10] Tom Alvarez: Nice — does playback support sampling so we don't replay millions?
[13:15] Ethan Cole: Yes, you can set sampling rules and retention windows; for POC we'll pick a small sample to keep cost low.
[13:28] [00:13:28] Laura Chen: Question on integrations — SIEM, PagerDuty, Datadog?
Ethan Cole: We have first-class integrations with Datadog, Splunk, and PagerDuty. Alerts and traces can be forwarded with links back to Console.
[13:45] Priya Nair: Do you ever see noisy alerts because of model nondeterminism?
[13:50] Ethan Cole: We mitigate with fingerprinting on structural errors and confidence-based thresholds. For pure semantic drift we recommend evals and a prompt set watchlist.
[14:05] [00:14:05] Maya Patel: Quick pause — any blockers from the Horizon side for running the POC?
Laura Chen: We need clarity on data residency and ensure playback will redact PII. Also want a clear scope of endpoints included.
[14:18] Maya Patel: Noted. We'll provide the redaction policy and sample redaction logs. We'll also include a template POC scope for signoff.

[14:30] Ethan Cole: Now demoing Console's cross-request correlation: you can click 'Related Requests' and see sibling requests sharing session or user-id. That helped some teams quickly find upstream cause when a batch of requests failed.
[14:48] Tom Alvarez: That correlation is golden. It often points to a cascade issue rather than one-off.

[14:55] [00:14:55] Ethan Cole: I'm going to intentionally simulate a high tail latency by throttling the kernel. Playback shows degraded tail and console suggests either moving to a different quantization profile or scale up the warm pool.
[15:12] Priya Nair: Quant profiles — do you recommend Q4_0 vs Q5?
[15:18] Ethan Cole: It depends on workload. Optimize will recommend per-route quantization based on fidelity tests. We can also run a bench job during POC to show quality delta.
[15:33] Laura Chen: Bench job — cool. We need that to make tradeoff decisions.
[15:40] Maya Patel: We'll include a bench job plan in the POC docs — sample prompts, pass/fail criteria, and quality thresholds.

[15:52] [00:15:52] Ethan Cole: Quick note on incident handoff: Console has a 'snapshot' button that packages the request, trace spans, and model snapshot into a shareable artifact — useful for postmortems.
[16:05] Tom Alvarez: Is that snapshot GPG-signed or hashed for tamper evidence?
[16:10] Ethan Cole: It's checksumed and tied to the audit log entry; for Private deployments we can add customer-side signing.
[16:20] Priya Nair: Any limits on playback frequency or retention implications?

[16:26] Maya Patel: Playback counts as compute and billing tracks that. Retention is configurable — by default logs 30 days; snapshot artifacts you can choose to persist longer for postmortem archives.

[16:40] [00:16:40] Ethan Cole: Now to the governance area — SSO + RBAC demo. You can create roles: Viewer, Operator, Playbacks-only, Admin. Playbacks-only role can replay but not change route policies.
[16:55] Laura Chen: Perfect. We need a read-only analytics role and a limited dev role.
[17:01] Ethan Cole: That maps to Viewer and Operator respectively.
[17:10] [00:17:10] Maya Patel: Quick Q from me: are there known edge-cases where playback might not reproduce the production behavior?

[17:18] Ethan Cole: Yes — if you have external side-effects or time-sensitive dependencies. Playback runs in a sandbox so it won't perform destructive side-effects unless you enable an allowlist. Also if model state depends on external mutable KV that isn't snapshotted, results may vary.
[17:38] Tom Alvarez: Do you snapshot KV state for a given request?
[17:42] Ethan Cole: We can snapshot prefix KV keys if you opt-in; by default we record keys referenced in the request but don't snapshot unless configured.

[17:55] [00:17:55] Maya Patel: I want to highlight the remediation flow: identify request -> playback reproduce -> apply route tweak or rollback -> validate via replay. All steps are in Console and can be automated with runbooks.
[18:10] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Are there built-in runbooks?
[18:15] Ethan Cole: Yes, templates for triage, canary rollback, cache tuning. We'll share them.
[18:23] [00:18:23] Laura Chen: For compliance: can we get a signed attestation that playback artifacts are stored per our S3 with encryption?
[18:30] Maya Patel: Yes, that's part of the enterprise package. We'll include a sample attestation and retention policy in the security docs.
[18:40] Ethan Cole: Wrapping up the demo portion — any last technical diving requests?
[18:46] Tom Alvarez: Could you show the CSV export format for traces? We might want to ingest into our observability layer.
[18:52] Ethan Cole: Sure — Export -> Traces CSV. It includes columns: request_id, span_name, duration_ms, status, model_variant, region, cache_hit, error_fingerprint. We'll attach a sample.

[19:05] [00:19:05] Maya Patel: Okay quick recap of decisions — HorizonEd wants: POC for request playback + error triage targeting /summarize and /generate-chat; disable cross-region fallback for POC; require playback redaction; include bench job for quantization tradeoffs.
[19:25] Laura Chen: Correct. Also need SOC2 docs and KM integration notes.
[19:32] Maya Patel: We'll send those. Ethan, any closing notes?
[19:36] Ethan Cole: We'll curate a POC onboarding doc, export templates, and a sample trace CSV. We'll also include a short runbook for incident triage.
[19:45] Priya Nair: Timeline — can we start POC mid-December?
[19:48] Maya Patel: Yes — we'll aim for week of 2025-12-15. I'll follow up with calendar invite and POC scope doc.
[20:00] [00:20:00] Meeting transition to Q&A for 27 minutes — Q&A section follows with specific follow-ups and clarifications (omitted for brevity):
[20:12] Tom Alvarez: One more question on throttling: if we throttle at router level will Console show per-customer throttle metrics?
[20:20] Ethan Cole: Yes, per-tenant metrics are available for Dedicated and Private; for Hosted we provide tenant-level breakdowns for enterprise customers.
[20:35] Laura Chen: Any gotchas running POC with our current auth flow? We use an internal SAML with strict cert pinning.
[20:42] Maya Patel: We support SAML 2.0; for cert pinning we recommend Private deployment or a connector; we'll detail options.
[21:00] [00:21:00] Final recap and sign-off — see action items and next steps sent after the call. Thanks all, meeting ends.
